course.title: Behavioral Economics
course.description: How real people actually decide — and where they predictably depart from the tidy 'rational agent'. Covers bounded rationality, cognitive biases, prospect theory, mental accounting, and the ethics of nudging. Built from openly-licensed OER Commons material (CC BY).

questions.prompt: Behavioral economics mainly studies…
options: how real people actually make decisions, including their systematic errors
how to maximize firm profit only
questions.explanation: It blends psychology and economics to explain how actual choices depart from the fully rational model — see 'Rational vs actual decisions'.

questions.prompt: 'Bounded rationality' means people…
options: make reasonable decisions within limits on information, time, and attention
questions.explanation: Herbert Simon's term: sensible choices under real cognitive and informational limits — not perfection, not chaos.

questions.prompt: Being unduly influenced by the first number you see is called…
questions.explanation: Anchoring — an initial value drags later estimates toward it. Covered in 'Cognitive biases'.

questions.prompt: Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind is the…
questions.explanation: The availability heuristic; vivid or recent events feel more probable than they are.

questions.prompt: Loss aversion is the finding that losses…
options: feel about the same as equivalent gains
feel roughly twice as painful as equivalent gains feel good
questions.explanation: Kahneman and Tversky estimated losses loom roughly twice as large as gains — central to prospect theory.

questions.prompt: Prospect theory says people evaluate outcomes relative to…
options: a reference point, such as the status quo
questions.explanation: Value is defined over gains and losses from a reference point, not over final wealth states.

questions.prompt: A 'nudge', as Thaler and Sunstein use the term, must…
options: steer choice while keeping all options open and easy to avoid
questions.explanation: A nudge alters the choice architecture without forbidding options or changing incentives much — see 'Nudges'.

questions.prompt: Treating money differently depending on where it 'came from' (a bonus vs. salary) is…
questions.explanation: Mental accounting — people file money into non-fungible mental buckets. Covered later in the course.

lessons.title: Rational agents vs. real people
lessons.grammar_note: Keep two labels straight: the 'econ' (fully rational model) vs. the 'human' (bounded, real).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what the standard rational-choice model assumes, and what 'bounded rationality' adds. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, does bounded rationality mean people are irrational?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Classical economics models a *rational agent* — sometimes called an 'econ' — who has stable preferences, weighs all options, and maximizes expected utility. It is a useful benchmark, not a photograph of reality. Herbert Simon argued that real deciders face limits on information, attention, and computing power, so they *satisfice*: they search until they find an option that is good enough rather than provably best. This is *bounded rationality* — reasonable behavior within real constraints, not randomness.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Choosing a laptop, the fully rational agent would compare every model on every spec. A real shopper reads three reviews, picks a 'good enough' machine, and stops. That is satisficing. It is not a failure — exhaustive search would cost more time than the better laptop is worth. The lesson: departures from the ideal model are often adaptive shortcuts, though the same shortcuts also produce predictable errors we study next.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Label each as closer to 'econ' or 'human': (1) reading every clause of a phone contract before signing, (2) ordering your 'usual' at a café without checking the menu, (3) picking the default retirement contribution rate. Answers: (1) econ, (2) human/satisficing, (3) human — defaults are accepted precisely because deciding is costly.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: hearing 'bounded rationality' as 'stupidity' — it means smart behavior under limits. Mistake: treating the rational model as wrong rather than as a benchmark. Exit: (a) What does a satisficer do instead of optimizing? (b) Name one real limit that bounds rationality. Answers: searches for a 'good enough' option and stops; time, information, or attention.

lessons.title: Cognitive biases: anchoring, availability, loss aversion
lessons.grammar_note: A heuristic is a shortcut; a bias is the systematic error the shortcut can cause.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define anchoring, the availability heuristic, and loss aversion, and spot each in the wild. Warm-up: which bias makes a plane crash feel scarier than it statistically is?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Kahneman and Tversky showed that useful mental shortcuts (*heuristics*) produce *systematic*, repeatable errors. *Anchoring*: an initial number pulls later estimates toward it, even when it is arbitrary. *Availability*: we judge frequency by how easily examples spring to mind, so vivid or recent events seem more common. *Loss aversion*: the pain of a loss is roughly twice the pleasure of an equal gain, so we work harder to avoid losses than to seek gains. These are patterns, not personal flaws — nearly everyone shows them.

sections.heading: Experiments & worked examples
sections.text: Anchoring: in a classic study, people spun a wheel rigged to stop at 10 or 65, then estimated the share of African nations in the UN — the higher spin produced markedly higher estimates, though the wheel was obviously random. Availability: people rate death by dramatic accidents as more likely than death by less newsworthy but far more common causes, because headlines are easy to recall. Loss aversion: the *endowment effect* — students given a mug demanded about twice as much to sell it as other students would pay to buy it, because giving it up registered as a loss.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Name the bias: (1) a $1,200 'original price' makes a $700 jacket feel cheap, (2) after a shark documentary you overrate the odds of a shark attack, (3) you refuse to sell concert tickets at face value but would never have paid that much today, (4) the first salary offer sets the whole negotiation range. Answers: (1) anchoring, (2) availability, (3) loss aversion / endowment effect, (4) anchoring.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling any mistake a 'bias' — a bias is a *systematic*, predictable one, not a one-off slip. Mistake: assuming experts are immune (they aren't). Exit: (a) Loss aversion says a loss feels about how many times an equal gain? (b) Which bias explains fearing rare, vivid dangers? Answers: about twice; the availability heuristic.

lessons.title: Prospect theory and framing
lessons.grammar_note: Reference point first, then gains vs. losses — value is always measured *from* somewhere.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain reference dependence, diminishing sensitivity, and how framing flips choices. Warm-up: if two options are mathematically identical, should wording change your pick?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Kahneman and Tversky's *prospect theory* (1979) replaced 'maximize final wealth' with three findings. (1) *Reference dependence*: outcomes are coded as gains or losses from a reference point, usually the status quo, not as absolute wealth. (2) *Diminishing sensitivity*: the difference between $10 and $20 feels bigger than between $1,010 and $1,020. (3) *Loss aversion*: the value curve is steeper for losses than for gains. Because the reference point is set by how a choice is *framed*, identical options described differently can reverse a decision.

sections.heading: Experiments & worked examples
sections.text: The 'Asian disease' problem: told a program 'saves 200 of 600', most people choose it (a sure gain); told the same program means '400 will die', most reject it (a sure loss) and gamble instead — yet the numbers are identical. The frame moved the reference point and flipped the choice. Everyday version: '90% lean' beef outsells '10% fat' beef; a 'card fee' repels shoppers a 'cash discount' of the same size does not.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For each pair, name the more appealing frame and the bias it exploits: (1) 'survival rate 90%' vs. 'mortality rate 10%', (2) 'earn a $5 bonus for paperless billing' vs. 'pay a $5 fee for paper billing'. Answers: (1) '90% survival' — a gain frame beats an equivalent loss frame; (2) the '$5 fee' framing deters more strongly because a fee reads as a loss (loss aversion).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking prospect theory is about money only — it applies to any coded gain or loss. Mistake: assuming framing is trickery every time; often it is unavoidable, which is exactly why it matters. Exit: (a) In prospect theory, value is measured relative to what? (b) Why can a gain frame and a loss frame of the same fact yield different choices? Answers: a reference point; because losses loom larger than equivalent gains.

questions.prompt: A satisficer, unlike a full optimizer,…
options: stops at the first 'good enough' option
questions.explanation: Satisficing is search-until-good-enough — the core of bounded rationality.

questions.prompt: An arbitrary spun-wheel number changing people's estimates demonstrates…
questions.explanation: The initial number anchors later judgments even when clearly random.

questions.prompt: The endowment effect (demanding more to sell than you'd pay to buy) is driven by…
questions.explanation: Giving the item up is coded as a loss, which looms larger.

questions.prompt: In prospect theory, outcomes are evaluated as gains or losses relative to a…
questions.explanation: Reference dependence is the theory's foundation.

questions.prompt: '90% lean' outselling '10% fat' beef is an example of…
questions.explanation: Logically identical, but the gain frame is more attractive.

questions.prompt: The availability heuristic makes people overestimate the risk of events that are…
questions.explanation: Ease of recall, not true frequency, drives the judgment.

lessons.title: Mental accounting
lessons.grammar_note: Money is 'fungible' — a dollar is a dollar. Mental accounting is what happens when we forget that.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain mental accounting and how it bends spending, saving, and the sunk-cost trap. Warm-up: is a $20 bill from your salary worth more or less than a $20 bill from a gift?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Richard Thaler's *mental accounting* describes how people sort money into separate, non-fungible mental 'accounts' — grocery money, fun money, a windfall — and treat each differently, even though economically a dollar is a dollar. This explains why a surprise bonus gets splurged while equal salary gets saved, why we keep a low-interest savings buffer while carrying high-interest card debt, and why the *sunk-cost fallacy* grips us: we 'charge' a past, unrecoverable payment to a mental account we hate to close at a loss.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Two theatergoers: one loses a $50 ticket at the door, one loses a $50 bill. The bill-loser usually still buys a ticket; the ticket-loser often goes home — buying 'again' feels like paying $100 for one show, because both charges hit the same 'theater' account. Sunk cost: finishing a bad movie 'because I paid for it' — the ticket money is gone either way, yet we stay to avoid booking the loss.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Spot the mental-accounting move: (1) saving a tax refund but spending an identical raise, (2) driving through a blizzard to a game 'because the tickets were expensive', (3) budgeting 'dining out' money so tightly you skip a cheap meal after payday. Answers: (1) windfalls and income sit in different accounts, (2) sunk-cost — the ticket cost is unrecoverable and irrelevant to the drive, (3) a rigid category cap overriding actual affordability.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming mental accounting is purely harmful — labeled 'save' jars also help people commit and avoid overspending. Mistake: confusing a sunk cost with a real future cost. Exit: (a) What property of money does mental accounting ignore? (b) Should a past, unrecoverable cost affect a forward-looking choice? Answers: fungibility; no — that's the sunk-cost fallacy.

lessons.title: Nudges and choice architecture — done ethically
lessons.grammar_note: A nudge keeps every option open; a mandate or ban does not. If it removes choice, it isn't a nudge.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define a nudge and choice architecture, give real applications in policy, marketing, and personal finance, and state when a nudge is ethical. Warm-up: does making the healthy option the default force anyone to eat it?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Every choice is presented in some layout — the order of options, the default, the wording. Thaler and Sunstein call whoever designs that layout the *choice architect*, and a *nudge* is any feature of it that predictably steers behavior *without* forbidding options or materially changing incentives. Defaults are the strongest nudge: because inertia and loss aversion make people stick with what's preset, switching a retirement plan to *automatic enrollment* (opt-out instead of opt-in) sharply raises participation while anyone remains free to leave. Their stance, 'libertarian paternalism', is that since some architecture is unavoidable, we may as well arrange it to help people meet their own goals.

sections.heading: Applications & the ethics test
sections.text: Policy: automatic pension enrollment; organ-donation defaults; 'Save More Tomorrow', which pre-commits raises to savings. Public health: placing fruit at eye level in a cafeteria. Personal finance: automatic transfers to savings on payday. Marketing uses the same levers — pre-ticked add-ons, drip pricing, fake scarcity — which is where ethics bite. Sunstein's test asks that a nudge be *transparent* (not hidden), preserve *freedom* to opt out easily, and serve the *chooser's* interests, not just the architect's. A default that helps you save and is easy to leave is an ethical nudge; a pre-checked insurance box buried at checkout is a *sludge* — friction engineered to exploit the same biases against you.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Ethical nudge or manipulative sludge? (1) auto-enrolling staff in a pension they can leave in one click, with the change announced, (2) a pre-ticked $9/month warranty the buyer must hunt to uncheck, (3) a countdown timer falsely claiming 'only 2 left', (4) defaulting a print dialog to double-sided while leaving single-sided one click away. Answers: (1) ethical — transparent, opt-out, serves the chooser; (2) sludge — hidden and self-serving; (3) manipulation — it fabricates scarcity; (4) ethical — a green default that's trivial to override.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling a ban or a fine a 'nudge' — nudges must leave options open and incentives roughly unchanged. Mistake: assuming any nudge is fine because it 'works'; effectiveness is not ethics. Exit: (a) Name Sunstein's three ethical conditions for a nudge. (b) What is 'sludge'? Answers: transparency, easy opt-out, and serving the chooser's own interests; friction designed to exploit biases against the chooser.

questions.prompt: Mental accounting violates which property of money?
questions.explanation: A dollar is a dollar regardless of its 'account' — that is fungibility.

questions.prompt: Continuing a bad project 'because we've already spent so much' is the…
questions.explanation: Past, unrecoverable costs should not drive forward-looking choices.

questions.prompt: For something to count as a nudge, it must…
options: keep all options open and easy to choose
questions.explanation: Nudges preserve freedom of choice and don't much change incentives.

questions.prompt: Automatic enrollment raises retirement-plan participation mainly because…
options: inertia and loss aversion make people accept the default
questions.explanation: Defaults harness inertia; people rarely switch away.

questions.prompt: 'Sludge' refers to…
options: a transparent, opt-out default that helps the chooser
friction engineered to exploit biases against the chooser
questions.explanation: Sludge weaponizes the same biases to serve the architect, not the chooser.

questions.prompt: Sunstein's ethical test for a nudge does NOT require that it…
options: guarantee everyone makes the same choice
questions.explanation: Ethical nudges keep choice open — uniform outcomes are not the goal.

lessons.title: Applied project: design an ethical nudge

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Choose one real decision people routinely make worse than they'd like — saving too little, skipping preventive health steps, wasting energy, overspending on subscriptions — and design a single nudge to improve it. You will not build it; you will specify it rigorously and defend it as ethical.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) State the decision and the specific bias in play (e.g., inertia, loss aversion, present bias). 2) Describe your nudge concretely — the default, wording, or layout you would change. 3) Predict the behavioral mechanism: exactly why it should work. 4) Run Sunstein's ethics test: is it transparent, is opting out easy, does it serve the chooser's own interests? 5) Name one way it could slide into 'sludge' and how you'd prevent that.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ You named a specific bias, not just 'people are lazy'. ✔ Your nudge keeps every option open and doesn't rely on a ban, fine, or hidden trick. ✔ The mechanism connects the bias to the design. ✔ You passed all three ethics conditions and could opt out in seconds. ✔ You honestly identified the sludge risk. If all five hold, you've designed like a responsible choice architect.
